heading: PROPHET NŪḤ (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ)
title: THE ARK OF PATIENCE
themes: Faith • Patience • Courage • Mercy • Trust in Allah
scope: 6 CONNECTED STORIES | 10 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 10 DAILY ACTIONS
reviewNote: For scholarly, linguistic, accessibility, and child-safeguarding review before publication
introduction: Volume Three continues the same Imaan & Akhlaq learning journey begun with Prophet Ādam (AS) and Prophet Idrīs (AS). The curious pen introduced at the end of the first volume, and the truth-checking habit developed in the second, now lead Imaan, Akhlaq, Mohsina and Sir Zameer to an Ark model in the school auditorium. The model is a contemporary classroom teaching aid, not an image of the actual Ark or a claim about its architecture.

The core existing children’s source was the revised story “The Ark of Patience: Doing the Right Thing When People Laugh,” which we reviewed alongside the older “Hazrat Nuh A.S Emaan and Ikhlaq” manuscript. This edition preserves the school and family setting, the Ark-model demonstration, and the principal patience-with-purpose message, while expanding the narrative into six linked fictional episodes and ten actionable learning missions.

stories.title: The Ship Beneath the Cloth
stories.subtitle: A mystery in the school auditorium

blocks.text: The narrow pen case from Uncle Sheikh still rested on the bookshelf. When Akhlaq opened it that morning, he found a note tucked beneath the lining. Dadi Jaan had written only three words: “The next journey.” Underneath was a tiny drawing of a ship.
“I knew it!” he exclaimed. “My pen is secretly a treasure map.”
Imaan leaned over the case. “It is a pen, Akhlaq. A very ordinary pen. Yesterday you used it to write your homework.”
“Every great adventure has to begin somewhere.”

At school, Mohsina was already waiting outside the auditorium. “Sir Zameer brought something huge,” she whispered. “The teachers carried it in under a blue cloth.” At that moment the bell rang, and the children hurried into the hall. A large shape stood at the centre of the stage. Sir Zameer greeted everyone with salām and, after the answer had echoed around the room, lifted the cloth.
A wooden ship model appeared. It had a broad body and a little mast that looked as if it would fall over in a strong breeze. Akhlaq gasped. “The Ark!”

“It is a model made for our lesson,” Sir Zameer corrected gently. “We do not know the Ark’s exact appearance from the Qur’an. But we know why Allah commanded Prophet Nūḥ, peace be upon him, to build it.”

Sir Zameer showed them a verse from Sūrat Nūḥ. Allah had sent Nūḥ to his people with a warning. He called them to worship Allah alone, to be mindful of Him, and to listen to the messenger sent to them. The children learned that the story began long before the waves. It began with the responsibility to speak the truth.
“Was his job easy?” Imaan asked.
“Not at all,” Sir Zameer said. “Many rejected him. His call was not about becoming popular. It was about obeying Allah and inviting people to what was right.”
Akhlaq watched the wooden model as though it might move. “Then why show us the ship first?”

“Because sometimes the ending catches our attention before we understand the beginning,” Sir Zameer replied. “And if you only remember a giant ship, you may miss the Prophet’s patience, his message, his prayer, and the people who listened or refused.”

After the session, the children returned to class. A new student had accidentally dropped his books in the corridor. Other pupils hurried past. Akhlaq hesitated: he was late for his favourite lesson. Then he remembered the teacher’s words about a message and a responsibility.
He crouched beside the boy and gathered the scattered notebooks. “You can take these. I’ve got the last two.”
He arrived a minute late, but with a clear explanation. His teacher thanked him for being helpful and reminded him to plan his time better next time.

That evening Dadi asked what the ship had taught him. “First,” Akhlaq replied, “I learned not to draw conclusions about a Prophet from a model. Second, even before a big journey, there can be a small thing that is right to do.”
Dadi lifted the little case. Inside, the pen now rested beside a small blue card marked with the number 950. “Then tomorrow,” she said, “you will learn why this number matters.”

blocks.label: EPISODE TAKEAWAY
blocks.text: Faith calls us to listen, learn, and act on what is right.
The number on the blue card had troubled Akhlaq all evening. “Nine hundred and fifty,” he repeated over breakfast. “That is more than nine hundred!”
“That is a very successful calculation,” Imaan said. “Now please finish your breakfast before it becomes a history lesson itself.”

At school, Sir Zameer displayed Sūrat Al-ʿAnkabūt 29:14 on the board. The Qur’an says Prophet Nūḥ remained among his people for a thousand years minus fifty. Sir Zameer explained that the verse described his long stay among them and was not a licence to invent other dates or a total lifespan.
“How could anyone keep trying for so long?” Mohsina asked.

“Listen to the way he described his effort,” the teacher replied. From Sūrat Nūḥ he showed how the Prophet called his people by night and by day, openly and privately. His concern was not a quick performance. It was a sustained act of obedience.

At the side of the classroom stood a table covered with paper, tape and three cups of water. The children had been asked to build a bridge that could support a small book. Imaan and Akhlaq worked with Mohsina and a new classmate, Hamza.
Their first bridge collapsed immediately. Their second folded when the book touched it. Akhlaq crushed the failed sheet in his fist. “This is impossible.”

Hamza said, “Maybe the problem is that you keep adding tape in the wrong place.” Akhlaq wanted to argue, but Imaan stopped him. “We can test it.” They measured the gap, folded the paper into beams and tried a third time. The book stayed in place.
Sir Zameer smiled. “Now compare what happened with just waiting.”
“We did not stand beside the paper and hope,” Mohsina answered. “We learned from the failures. We changed the design.”

“This is one small modern example of persistent work,” Sir Zameer said. “But do not imagine that our classroom project measures the immense patience of a Prophet. His duty and the opposition he faced were far greater. The analogy only helps us practise an ordinary part of steadfastness.”
Later, a classmate laughed at the shape of the bridge. It looked lopsided, and one corner was covered in extra tape. Hamza flushed red. Akhlaq began preparing a sharp reply, but Imaan shook her head.
“Is it safe? Does it hold the book?” she asked. The classmate tested it and nodded. “Then we can still improve how it looks.”

When they presented the project, each child described one mistake and one improvement. Nobody claimed to have solved everything at the first attempt. Sir Zameer placed the blue card at the front of the table. The number 950 was not a game score; it was a reminder that the Qur’an records extraordinary perseverance.
At home, Akhlaq wanted to add a new number to his notebook: “Three.”
“Only three?” Dadi asked.
“Three attempts,” Akhlaq replied. “I know it is a tiny number beside 950. But it is the first time I nearly gave up and then tried to learn instead.”
Dadi smiled. “Then your learning has begun.”

blocks.label: EPISODE TAKEAWAY
blocks.text: Patience includes responsible effort and learning from mistakes.

The next afternoon, Sir Zameer switched off the classroom lights and projected a sky filled with stars. There was no frightening sound and no hidden secret to uncover. Just the wide night sky, the sun, the moon and pictures of green gardens, rain and growing plants.
Akhlaq leaned toward Imaan. “Are we going to space instead of the Ark?”

“We are going to read another part of the same message,” Sir Zameer answered. He explained that Prophet Nūḥ reminded his people to recognise Allah’s majesty and the signs of His creation. He also called them to ask Allah for forgiveness. Sūrat Nūḥ speaks of rain, gardens and provision as blessings under Allah’s authority.
“Does that mean if I say astaghfirullāh, I get better marks tomorrow?” a child asked.

“No,” Sir Zameer replied. “We do not turn the Qur’an into a trick for obtaining specific rewards on our timetable. We seek Allah’s forgiveness because we need His mercy and want to correct ourselves. Allah grants blessings with His own wisdom.”

The class divided into teams for a short presentation. Imaan’s group was assigned the sky. Mohsina chose plants. A shy boy called Rafi had been assigned water, but his poster was plain. When he opened his notebook, another student whispered, “He does not even have colored markers.”
Mohsina heard it. She turned around. “Our lesson is not about whose poster is more expensive. Rafi has collected excellent facts.”

Sir Zameer used that moment to explain that some of Nūḥ’s opponents looked down on those who followed him. The Qur’anic criticism of such arrogance was a warning against judging people by wealth or social position. “We must respect people,” he said, “whether they have new markers, old notebooks, fancy shoes, or none of those things.”

When it was Rafi’s turn, his voice was so quiet the microphone hardly picked it up. Akhlaq moved the microphone closer, then stepped back so Rafi could speak. He had prepared three observations: how plants need water, how clouds move, and how a small seed grows. As the class listened, Imaan noticed the careful drawings along the bottom of his page.
Afterwards she said, “I had not looked closely before. Those drawings are wonderful.”
Rafi grinned. “I used a pencil. I can draw them again if you want.”

During the final activity, each child wrote one thing they were grateful for on a leaf-shaped card. The cards formed a paper tree at the front of the classroom. Akhlaq wrote, “People who help when I cannot do something alone.”

The children’s learning notebook now had another heading: “WHAT THE QUR’AN TEACHES.” Under it they wrote Tawḥīd, repentance, gratitude, and the dignity of people. On the next page they wrote “WHAT WE MUST NOT INVENT.” It included the names of unverified Ark builders and the exact number of floors.
When Imaan told Dadi about Rafi, her grandmother asked, “Did your kindness make a difference?”
“Maybe,” Imaan said. “But Rafi’s good work was already there. We had to learn to notice it.”

blocks.label: EPISODE TAKEAWAY
blocks.text: Seek Allah’s forgiveness, notice His blessings, and respect every person.

stories.title: Build While They Laugh
stories.subtitle: A model, a command, and the courage to continue

blocks.text: On Thursday, the great wooden ship model was back on Sir Zameer’s table. This time, he had placed a ruler beside it and drawn a large question mark on the board.
“How many floors did the real Ark have?” he asked.

Hands shot up. One student said three. Another said seven. A third insisted it must have been as tall as a building. Sir Zameer waited until everyone was quiet. “The Qur’an tells us that Allah commanded Nūḥ to build the Ark under His watch and revelation. It does not give us the complete floor plan. So the truthful answer to my question is: we do not know from the Qur’an.”
He read the Qur’anic passage about Nūḥ building the ship while chiefs of his people passed and mocked him. There was laughter around him, yet he continued the task Allah had commanded.
“Did he reply?” Akhlaq asked.
“The Qur’an records his answer,” Sir Zameer said. He explained its meaning without adding invented words. “His reply warned them that their mockery did not change the truth of Allah’s decree.”

That afternoon the school hosted a small exhibition. Each team had to construct something that could float safely in a basin. Imaan’s group chose folded card reinforced with tape. A passing classmate burst into laughter. “That will sink before you put it in the water.”
For a moment Akhlaq wished he could hide the project behind his bag. Hamza looked ready to argue. Mohsina simply held the boat level while Imaan checked its edges.
“We can listen if he has a useful suggestion,” she said, “but laughing is not a reason to abandon our work.”
They floated the boat. It tilted, took in a little water and sank. The laughing boy shouted, “I told you!” Akhlaq’s ears burned. Sir Zameer handed them a towel and said, “What did the test reveal?”
“The paper is too thin on one side,” Akhlaq answered reluctantly.
“Then change that,” Sir Zameer replied.

They built again. Their second model stayed afloat much longer. It did not win the exhibition, but the team could explain why it improved. The classmate who had laughed eventually came over. “Could I try the same fold?” he asked. Akhlaq nodded and showed him where the paper had first failed.

When the hall was empty, Sir Zameer closed the lesson. “There is a difference between being mocked because you are doing what is right and being corrected because you actually need to improve. A wise learner checks the evidence, listens to helpful criticism, and continues without allowing humiliation to control the decision.”
At home, Akhlaq put the damp paper boat beside the little pen case. “We should save it,” he said.
“Why?” Imaan asked. “It looks dreadful.”
“Because it was our first attempt. If we throw it away, we might forget what we learned.”
Dadi looked at the patched little boat and said, “That is a better treasure than pretending you never made a mistake.”

blocks.label: EPISODE TAKEAWAY
blocks.text: Respond to mockery with evidence, steadiness, and respectful improvement.

stories.title: The Waves and a Father’s Call
stories.subtitle: A serious part of the story, taught with care

blocks.text: On Friday the classroom curtains were drawn again, but Sir Zameer did not uncover the Ark model immediately. He placed a small card on every seat. It read: “Some stories have sad moments. You may ask a question, take a pause, or speak to a trusted adult.”
“We are going to hear a difficult part of Nūḥ’s story,” he explained. “Please listen respectfully.”

He showed the verses describing the arrival of Allah’s command. Those whom Allah instructed Nūḥ to take aboard entered the Ark. The ship moved through waves that the Qur’an compared to mountains. Nūḥ called to a son who was apart from the believers, inviting him to board. The son believed a mountain would protect him, but no ordinary refuge could protect anyone from Allah’s decree that day. The waves came between them, and the son drowned.
The hall became still. Mohsina looked at the little model without speaking. Akhlaq moved closer to Imaan.
“Why did the son not come?” a student asked softly.
“The Qur’an tells us his reply,” Sir Zameer said, “but we must not pretend we know every thought in his heart. The passage teaches that even a loving father cannot force another person to believe.”
“Did Nūḥ feel sad?” Imaan asked.

“The Qur’an records his call and his concern for his son,” the teacher replied. “We should speak gently about this sorrow. It is not a scene for dramatic sound effects or a game in which someone loses points.”
Akhlaq looked puzzled. “What does this teach us at school?”

“It teaches several things,” Sir Zameer said. “Trust Allah, listen to true guidance, and do not mistake our own guesses for certainty. We also have an everyday duty to follow real safety instructions. When there is a dangerous situation at home or school, find a trusted adult and follow the safety plan. Do not try to prove you are brave by ignoring warnings.”

They practised a calm classroom evacuation routine with the teacher, walking without pushing and waiting at the marked gathering place. Nobody pretended that the school activity was the same as the Flood, and no child was assigned the role of Nūḥ’s son. The exercise was simply a modern responsibility the children could learn from the principle of listening and acting wisely.

When the class returned, Sir Zameer explained that the Qur’an also tells of Nūḥ asking Allah about his son and being taught that relationship alone does not override Allah’s judgment. Nūḥ responded with humility and asked for forgiveness and mercy. These are serious teachings, not reasons for children to distrust loving families or fear that an ordinary mistake would cause such punishment.
That evening Dadi placed a small blue piece of fabric beneath the wooden model at home. “Would you like to tell me what troubled you?” she asked.
Akhlaq hesitated. “I felt sad for a father calling to his son.”
“That is a compassionate response,” Dadi replied. “We can learn Allah’s guidance and still recognize that this is a sorrowful part of the account.”
Imaan folded the fabric carefully. “I’m glad Sir Zameer let us ask questions.”
“Good teachers make room for thoughtful questions,” Dadi said. “And good learners ask with respect.”

blocks.label: EPISODE TAKEAWAY
blocks.text: Trust Allah, follow true guidance, and be gentle when discussing grief.
The last session began with silence and a picture of a calm mountain landscape. In front of it, Sir Zameer placed the same wooden ship model, no longer surrounded by blue paper waves.
“The Qur’an tells us how the Flood ended,” he said. “Allah commanded the earth to swallow its water and the sky to stop. The waters subsided, and the Ark came to rest on al-Jūdī.”
Mohsina leaned forward. “So the story ends here?”

“Not quite. Allah granted peace and blessings to Nūḥ and those with him. The Qur’an teaches us that after rescue there is also responsibility: to remember Allah, live with gratitude, and continue in what is right.”

Sir Zameer showed the class the supplication of Nūḥ in which he sought forgiveness for himself, his parents and the believing men and women. He also pointed out that the complete verse contains a concluding prayer concerning persistent wrongdoers in its own historical context. “When children memorise a suitable portion,” he explained, “we choose an excerpt carefully and never direct a prayer of destruction at classmates or people who upset us.”

The class had one final task: create an “Ark of Good Choices” display. Each learner could add a card naming an action they would practise—not a promise they were afraid to break, and not a public confession of a private mistake.
Imaan wrote: “Listen when someone is explaining something important.”
Mohsina wrote: “Never laugh at another child’s struggle.”
Hamza wrote: “Try a new method instead of giving up.”
Rafi drew a small green leaf and wrote: “Be thankful for what I can learn.”

Akhlaq sat with his pen poised over an empty card. His first idea was very grand: “I will always be patient, never be upset, and never make another mistake.” But he scratched it out. It was too big to be honest.
He wrote something smaller: “When I make an error in a task, I will look for one useful correction.”

As the children fixed their cards to the display, Sir Zameer called each group to the front. He did not announce whose faith was strongest, whose good deeds were worth most, or which student was “closest to a Prophet.” Instead, the class spoke about the things they had learned and the kindness they hoped to practise.

At home, Dadi placed the pen case and the little blue card marked 950 into the wooden box. Then she brought out a new envelope. It was brown, decorated with a strong stone tower and a single word: “HUD.”
“Another ship?” Akhlaq asked.
“No,” Dadi replied. “Another people. Another messenger. Another lesson about what happens when people mistake strength for the right to be arrogant.”

Imaan looked at the Ark model one last time. She had thought its greatest lesson would be about surviving an enormous flood. Now she understood that the story had begun with worshipping Allah, continued through patient work and truthful warning, and ended with a reminder to stay humble and grateful.
“Then we should keep the wooden box,” she said.
Dadi nodded. “Of course. We have only just begun to learn.”

blocks.label: EPISODE TAKEAWAY
blocks.text: After a hard chapter, practise gratitude, humility and useful goodness.

missions.title: A Messenger with a Clear Message

discover.label: LINKED STORY
discover.text: Story 1 | PRIMARY REVELATION: Nūḥ 71:1–4

discover.label: Character objective
discover.text: Tawḥīd, listening and the responsibility to advise with care
إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحًا إِلَىٰ قَوْمِهِ أَنْ أَنْذِرْ قَوْمَكَ مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ
Qur’an 71:1 | Working meaning: Allah sent Nūḥ to warn his people before painful punishment came to them.
قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ إِنِّي لَكُمْ نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ
Qur’an 71:2 | Working meaning: Nūḥ addressed his people with a clear warning.
Understand the guidance

Allah sent Nūḥ to his people to call them to worship Allah alone, take His guidance seriously, and turn away from wrongdoing. The warning was part of a messenger’s duty; it was not a child deciding to punish someone. We can learn to speak respectfully about right and wrong, but the Qur’anic message is much greater than a classroom rule. A kind invitation does not change what is true.

discover.label: Imaan & Akhlaq
discover.text: fictional decision scene
Imaan notices that a younger student cannot find the classroom. She is tempted to hurry past because her own bell is about to ring. Akhlaq reminds her that giving a clear, kind direction can matter.

missions.question: What is the best response when you can help someone understand a simple classroom instruction?

choices.text: Laugh because the student should already know.
Give a short, clear answer and, if needed, ask the teacher to help.
choices.feedback: A respectful explanation is more helpful than mockery or pretending. Unlike a Prophet’s divinely given message, our everyday advice must be based on what we actually know.

choices.text: Invent an answer so you sound knowledgeable.

missions.action: Explain one true, useful instruction kindly to someone who needs it today.

remember.label: A moment to reflect
remember.text: Did my words make it easier for someone to understand what to do?

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: نَذِير (nadhīr): warner; قَوْم (qawm): people

missions.title: Nine Hundred and Fifty: Patient Effort

discover.label: LINKED STORY
discover.text: Story 2 | PRIMARY REVELATION: Al-ʿAnkabūt 29:14

discover.label: Character objective
discover.text: Perseverance without exaggerating historical facts
وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحًا إِلَىٰ قَوْمِهِ فَلَبِثَ فِيهِمْ أَلْفَ سَنَةٍ إِلَّا خَمْسِينَ عَامًا فَأَخَذَهُمُ الطُّوفَانُ وَهُمْ ظَالِمُونَ
Qur’an 29:14 | Working meaning: Nūḥ remained among his people for one thousand years minus fifty, and the Flood overtook them while they persisted in wrongdoing.
Understand the guidance

The Qur’an records that Nūḥ remained among his people for one thousand years less fifty. This is a statement about his stay among his people, not a full biography with every date. Their persistent refusal did not make his message false. Children should understand that patient obedience is not the same as obtaining immediate approval. In ordinary learning, patience means taking sensible steps and seeking support where needed, rather than enduring harm silently.

discover.label: Imaan & Akhlaq
discover.text: fictional decision scene
Akhlaq’s paper bridge falls twice during a group challenge. He is ready to tear the pages and quit while Mohsina suggests measuring the gap and changing the fold.

missions.question: What is a patient, responsible next step?

choices.text: Give up and blame the others.
Tell the group that the first bridge was perfect even though it collapsed.
Check why it failed, agree on one improvement, and test again.
choices.feedback: Patience is joined with useful action. A classroom task is a small practice, not a comparison with the centuries of Prophetic perseverance.

missions.action: Choose one safe learning task and try one improved method after a mistake.

remember.label: A moment to reflect
remember.text: What did I change after my first attempt?

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: لَبِثَ (labitha): remained; عَام (ʿām): year

missions.title: Day and Night: More Than One Way to Explain

discover.label: LINKED STORY
discover.text: Story 2 | PRIMARY REVELATION: Nūḥ 71:5–9

discover.label: Character objective
discover.text: Steadfastness and respectful communication
قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي دَعَوْتُ قَوْمِي لَيْلًا وَنَهَارًا
Qur’an 71:5 | Working meaning: Nūḥ said he had called his people by night and by day.
Understand the guidance

Nūḥ told Allah that he had called his people by night and by day. The Qur’an also describes public and private invitation, while recording how many people rejected him. This is not an instruction for children to keep pressing another child after a refusal. We can learn to choose an appropriate time, use a gentle tone, and ask for help when someone is distressed. A person’s responsibility is to offer truthful goodness; results remain with Allah.

discover.label: Imaan & Akhlaq
discover.text: fictional decision scene
Imaan is helping Rafi read a page. He becomes overwhelmed when several classmates speak at once. Instead of repeating the same words louder, Imaan offers to point to the next line and give him time.

missions.question: How should Imaan respond?

choices.text: Slow down, ask what would help, and give Rafi space.
choices.feedback: Different people may need different respectful explanations. Pressuring, shaming or exposing difficulties is not helpful.

choices.text: Speak louder until he agrees.
Announce that Rafi is slow so others will stop asking.

missions.action: Practise explaining one idea calmly, then check whether the other person understands.

remember.label: A moment to reflect
remember.text: Did I listen as carefully as I spoke?

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: دَعَوْتُ (daʿawtu): I called/invited; لَيْلًا (laylan): at night

missions.title: The Open Door of Forgiveness

discover.label: LINKED STORY
discover.text: Story 3 | PRIMARY REVELATION: Nūḥ 71:10–12

discover.label: Character objective
discover.text: Istighfār, accountability, hope
فَقُلْتُ اسْتَغْفِرُوا رَبَّكُمْ إِنَّهُ كَانَ غَفَّارًا
Qur’an 71:10 | Working meaning: He invited them to seek forgiveness from their Lord, who is abundantly forgiving.
Understand the guidance

Nūḥ invited his people to seek Allah’s forgiveness and reminded them of His generosity. The verses mention blessings such as rain and gardens. They must not be presented as a mechanical promise that saying a formula guarantees grades, prizes or money on demand. Genuine repentance means acknowledging wrongdoing, asking Allah for forgiveness and trying to leave the wrongdoing. Where another person has been harmed, making amends matters too.

discover.label: Imaan & Akhlaq
discover.text: fictional decision scene
Akhlaq borrows Mohsina’s colored pencil without asking and accidentally breaks its tip. He thinks a whispered apology to Allah is enough and considers returning it without saying anything.

missions.question: What is the best next step?

choices.text: Hide it and tell nobody.
Ask Allah for forgiveness, tell Mohsina the truth, and help replace or repair it.
choices.feedback: Seeking Allah’s forgiveness should move us toward truth and repair, not away from responsibility.

choices.text: Pretend another child broke it.

missions.action: Correct one small mistake today by honestly apologizing and trying to make it right.

remember.label: A moment to reflect
remember.text: What did I learn about the difference between saying sorry and changing my action?

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: اسْتَغْفِرُوا (istaghfirū): seek forgiveness; غَفَّار (ghaffār): abundantly forgiving

missions.title: Look Up, Look Around: Signs of Allah

discover.label: LINKED STORY
discover.text: Story 3 | PRIMARY REVELATION: Nūḥ 71:13–20

discover.label: Character objective
discover.text: Reverence, gratitude and responsible observation
مَا لَكُمْ لَا تَرْجُونَ لِلَّهِ وَقَارًا
Qur’an 71:13 | Working meaning: Why do you not regard Allah with the reverence due to Him?
Understand the guidance

Nūḥ directed his people’s attention to the majesty of Allah and to the creation around them. His message was religious guidance, not a science textbook with a list of modern discoveries. Observing rain, plants, stars and the earth can deepen gratitude and reflection. A child should be encouraged to ask genuine questions and learn patiently, without inventing details about creation that the verses do not state.

discover.label: Imaan & Akhlaq
discover.text: fictional decision scene
The class creates a paper tree of things they appreciate. Imaan writes “the person who helps me learn” rather than “the person who buys the most expensive supplies.”

missions.question: What would make an appropriate gratitude card?

choices.text: “I am grateful for rain and the people who help me.”
choices.feedback: Gratitude helps us notice Allah’s gifts without boasting about possessions.

choices.text: “My poster is more important because it is expensive.”
“I only care about blessings I can show off.”

missions.action: Notice one blessing in nature and thank Allah for it once today.

remember.label: A moment to reflect
remember.text: How can a blessing become a reason for kindness rather than showing off?

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: وَقَارًا (waqāran): reverence/majesty

missions.title: People Matter More Than Status

discover.label: LINKED STORY
discover.text: Story 3 | PRIMARY REVELATION: Al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:111–115; Hūd 11:27

discover.label: Character objective
discover.text: Human dignity and rejection of social arrogance
قَالُوا أَنُؤْمِنُ لَكَ وَاتَّبَعَكَ الْأَرْذَلُونَ
Qur’an 26:111 | Working meaning: His opponents objected because they looked down upon those who had followed him.
Understand the guidance

Some opponents of Nūḥ dismissed those who followed him and looked down on people they saw as low in status. The Qur’anic account exposes the arrogance of judging a message by the social position of its followers. This does not mean the Prophet asked children to ignore genuine evidence or safety; it means money, popularity and outward appearance do not establish human worth. Our real-life mission is to include people respectfully.

discover.label: Imaan & Akhlaq
discover.text: fictional decision scene

Rafi has an excellent science explanation but his presentation uses an old notebook. One pupil whispers that his work will not be good because he lacks expensive markers. Imaan sees that the drawings are careful and accurate.

missions.question: How should Imaan respond?

choices.text: Judge the notebook by its cover.
Repeat the unkind comment to the class.
Invite Rafi to explain his work and judge the explanation fairly.
choices.feedback: Knowledge and dignity are not measured by possessions or popularity.

missions.action: Include or encourage one person who is being overlooked today.

remember.label: A moment to reflect
remember.text: Have I ever confused someone’s belongings with their abilities?

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: اتَّبَعَكَ (ittabaʿaka): followed you

missions.title: Build Under Allah’s Care

discover.label: LINKED STORY
discover.text: Story 4 | PRIMARY REVELATION: Hūd 11:36–37

discover.label: Character objective
discover.text: Tawakkul with purposeful effort and obedience
وَاصْنَعِ الْفُلْكَ بِأَعْيُنِنَا وَوَحْيِنَا وَلَا تُخَاطِبْنِي فِي الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا إِنَّهُمْ مُغْرَقُونَ
Qur’an 11:37 | Working meaning: Allah commanded Nūḥ to build the Ark under divine care and revelation; judgment on the wrongdoing people was decreed.
Understand the guidance

Allah commanded Nūḥ to build the Ark under divine care and revelation. The Qur’an establishes the command, but it does not give a complete engineering design. Trust in Allah is not an excuse for refusing the work entrusted to us. In a child’s life, trust and responsibility can appear in preparing properly, asking for skilled help, using safe materials and completing a task honestly. We do not pretend a school craft is equivalent to Prophetic obedience.

discover.label: Imaan & Akhlaq
discover.text: fictional decision scene
Akhlaq wants his model boat to float but refuses to follow the teacher’s simple safety rules. Mohsina asks him to read the instructions first and test it in the supervised basin.

missions.question: What combines responsible work with trust?

choices.text: Follow instructions, work carefully, ask for help and trust Allah.
choices.feedback: Tawakkul belongs with lawful, sensible effort; it is not carelessness.

choices.text: Ignore the rules because “Allah will protect us.”
Let others do all the work and claim the result.

missions.action: Prepare properly for one responsibility today before beginning it.

remember.label: A moment to reflect
remember.text: What preparation did I complete instead of relying on a wish?

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: الْفُلْك (al-fulk): the ship/Ark; وَحْي (waḥy): revelation

missions.title: Steady When Others Laugh

discover.label: LINKED STORY
discover.text: Story 4 | PRIMARY REVELATION: Hūd 11:38–39

discover.label: Character objective
discover.text: Courage, self-control and wise response to mockery
وَيَصْنَعُ الْفُلْكَ وَكُلَّمَا مَرَّ عَلَيْهِ مَلَأٌ مِنْ قَوْمِهِ سَخِرُوا مِنْهُ قَالَ إِنْ تَسْخَرُوا مِنَّا فَإِنَّا نَسْخَرُ مِنْكُمْ كَمَا تَسْخَرُونَ
Qur’an 11:38 | Working meaning: As Nūḥ built the Ark, leaders of his people mocked him; he answered their mockery with a warning of what would come.
Understand the guidance

The Qur’an describes leaders of Nūḥ’s people mocking him as he built the Ark. His response is recorded in the verse and belongs to the solemn setting of divine judgment. Children must not copy it as a licence to threaten or taunt peers. A modern lesson is that mockery does not settle whether something is true. We should check our facts, accept constructive criticism, avoid retaliation and seek trusted adult support in bullying situations.

discover.label: Imaan & Akhlaq
discover.text: fictional decision scene
A classmate laughs because Imaan’s boat sinks in a test. She can either insult him back or ask the team to identify one design problem.

missions.question: What is the wisest response?

choices.text: Mock the classmate’s family.
Ask for one useful correction and keep working without insults.
choices.feedback: A calm response protects dignity and allows improvement. Bullying should be reported rather than endured in silence.

choices.text: Delete the project and tell everyone it was stolen.

missions.action: Respond calmly to one minor criticism; if it is bullying, tell a trusted adult.

remember.label: A moment to reflect
remember.text: How can I tell the difference between unkind mockery and helpful correction?

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: سَخِرُوا (sakhirū): they mocked

missions.title: The Waves and a Father’s Call

discover.label: LINKED STORY
discover.text: Story 5 | PRIMARY REVELATION: Hūd 11:40–43

discover.label: Character objective
discover.text: Trust in Allah, taking warnings seriously, care in grief
وَقَالَ ارْكَبُوا فِيهَا بِسْمِ اللَّهِ مَجْرَاهَا وَمُرْسَاهَا إِنَّ رَبِّي لَغَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ
Qur’an 11:41 | Working meaning: Nūḥ instructed them to board in Allah’s name, acknowledging that Allah governs its sailing and resting.
وَهِيَ تَجْرِي بِهِمْ فِي مَوْجٍ كَالْجِبَالِ وَنَادَىٰ نُوحٌ ابْنَهُ وَكَانَ فِي مَعْزِلٍ يَا بُنَيَّ ارْكَبْ مَعَنَا وَلَا تَكُنْ مَعَ الْكَافِرِينَ
Qur’an 11:42 | Working meaning: The Ark moved through enormous waves; Nūḥ called tenderly to his son to come aboard.
قَالَ سَآوِي إِلَىٰ جَبَلٍ يَعْصِمُنِي مِنَ الْمَاءِ قَالَ لَا عَاصِمَ الْيَوْمَ مِنْ أَمْرِ اللَّهِ إِلَّا مَنْ رَحِمَ وَحَالَ بَيْنَهُمَا الْمَوْجُ فَكَانَ مِنَ الْمُغْرَقِينَ
Qur’an 11:43 | Working meaning: His son thought a mountain would protect him; the waves came between them and he was among those who drowned.
Understand the guidance

When the Flood came, those whom Allah commanded were brought aboard. The Ark sailed in the name of Allah. Nūḥ called tenderly to a son who was separated from him, but the son turned to a mountain that could not protect him from Allah’s decree. The Qur’an states that he drowned. This is a grave episode about faith, divine judgment and family sorrow. Do not tell children that a normal mistake or disagreement with parents is comparable to this event. A careful practical lesson is to heed reliable safety guidance and show compassion to the distressed.

discover.label: Imaan & Akhlaq
discover.text: fictional decision scene
During a school safety drill, the teacher tells the class to walk to a gathering point. Akhlaq wants to take an unsafe shortcut because he thinks he knows a faster route.

missions.question: What should Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Follow the supervised route calmly and help a classmate stay with the group.
choices.feedback: Safety guidance is followed calmly; kindness helps everyone. The drill is a practical analogy, not a reenactment of the Flood.

choices.text: Run away alone to prove he is brave.
Laugh at anyone who feels frightened.

missions.action: Learn or review one genuine safety instruction with a trusted adult today.

remember.label: A moment to reflect
remember.text: How can I help someone who feels worried during an emergency?

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: ارْكَب (irkab): board; مَوْج (mawj): waves

missions.title: After the Water: Gratitude and Humility

discover.label: LINKED STORY
discover.text: Story 6 | PRIMARY REVELATION: Hūd 11:44–49; Nūḥ 71:28

discover.label: Character objective
discover.text: Gratitude, humility, duʿāʾ and responsible new beginnings
وَقِيلَ يَا أَرْضُ ابْلَعِي مَاءَكِ وَيَا سَمَاءُ أَقْلِعِي وَغِيضَ الْمَاءُ وَقُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ وَاسْتَوَتْ عَلَى الْجُودِيِّ وَقِيلَ بُعْدًا لِلْقَوْمِ الظَّالِمِينَ
Qur’an 11:44 | Working meaning: The water subsided, the decree was fulfilled, and the Ark came to rest on al-Jūdī.
قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ أَنْ أَسْأَلَكَ مَا لَيْسَ لِي بِهِ عِلْمٌ وَإِلَّا تَغْفِرْ لِي وَتَرْحَمْنِي أَكُنْ مِنَ الْخَاسِرِينَ
Qur’an 11:47 | Working meaning: Nūḥ sought refuge in Allah from asking about what he did not know and asked for forgiveness and mercy.
رَبِّ اغْفِرْ لِي وَلِوَالِدَيَّ وَلِمَنْ دَخَلَ بَيْتِيَ مُؤْمِنًا وَلِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتِ وَلَا تَزِدِ الظَّالِمِينَ إِلَّا تَبَارًا
Qur’an 71:28 | Working meaning: Nūḥ prayed for forgiveness for himself, his parents and the believers; the concluding plea against wrongdoers belongs to its historical context.
Understand the guidance

Allah commanded the water to subside, and the Ark rested on al-Jūdī. Later verses speak of peace and blessings, and they show Nūḥ asking Allah for mercy and seeking refuge from speaking without knowledge. His supplication in Sūrat Nūḥ also asks forgiveness for his parents and believers. Children should memorize a suitable, clearly identified excerpt if able, without directing the verse’s concluding prayer against wrongdoers at peers. After difficulty, gratitude is joined with renewed responsibility.

discover.label: Imaan & Akhlaq
discover.text: fictional decision scene

At the final class exhibition, Akhlaq first writes “I will never make mistakes again” on his character card. Then he crosses it out and chooses a smaller honest promise: “When I make an error, I will try one correction.”

missions.question: Which completion card shows sincere learning?

choices.text: “I am better than the children who got fewer points.”
“I have reached perfect faith.”
“I will practise one small act of gratitude and responsible effort.”
choices.feedback: We do not measure faith with a leaderboard. A sincere, achievable action is more helpful than boasting or claiming perfection.

missions.action: Thank Allah for one blessing and use that blessing in a helpful way today.

remember.label: A moment to reflect
remember.text: What would I like to carry forward from all six stories?

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: الْجُودِيّ (al-Jūdī): the mountain named in the verse; اغْفِر (ighfir): forgive

review.arabic: إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحًا إِلَىٰ قَوْمِهِ أَنْ أَنْذِرْ قَوْمَكَ مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ
review.meaning: Allah sent Nūḥ to warn his people before painful punishment came to them.

review.arabic: قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ إِنِّي لَكُمْ نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ
review.meaning: Nūḥ addressed his people with a clear warning.

review.arabic: وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحًا إِلَىٰ قَوْمِهِ فَلَبِثَ فِيهِمْ أَلْفَ سَنَةٍ إِلَّا خَمْسِينَ عَامًا فَأَخَذَهُمُ الطُّوفَانُ وَهُمْ ظَالِمُونَ
review.meaning: Nūḥ remained among his people for one thousand years minus fifty, and the Flood overtook them while they persisted in wrongdoing.

review.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي دَعَوْتُ قَوْمِي لَيْلًا وَنَهَارًا
review.meaning: Nūḥ said he had called his people by night and by day.

review.arabic: فَقُلْتُ اسْتَغْفِرُوا رَبَّكُمْ إِنَّهُ كَانَ غَفَّارًا

review.meaning: As Nūḥ built the Ark, leaders of his people mocked him; he answered their mockery with a warning of what would come.

review.arabic: قَالَ سَآوِي إِلَىٰ جَبَلٍ يَعْصِمُنِي مِنَ الْمَاءِ قَالَ لَا عَاصِمَ الْيَوْمَ مِنْ أَمْرِ اللَّهِ إِلَّا مَنْ رَحِمَ وَحَالَ بَيْنَهُمَا الْمَوْجُ فَكَانَ مِنَ الْمُغْرَقِينَ
review.meaning: His son thought a mountain would protect him; the waves came between them and he was among those who drowned.

review.arabic: وَقِيلَ يَا أَرْضُ ابْلَعِي مَاءَكِ وَيَا سَمَاءُ أَقْلِعِي وَغِيضَ الْمَاءُ وَقُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ وَاسْتَوَتْ عَلَى الْجُودِيِّ وَقِيلَ بُعْدًا لِلْقَوْمِ الظَّالِمِينَ
review.meaning: The water subsided, the decree was fulfilled, and the Ark came to rest on al-Jūdī.

review.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ أَنْ أَسْأَلَكَ مَا لَيْسَ لِي بِهِ عِلْمٌ وَإِلَّا تَغْفِرْ لِي وَتَرْحَمْنِي أَكُنْ مِنَ الْخَاسِرِينَ
review.meaning: Nūḥ sought refuge in Allah from asking about what he did not know and asked for forgiveness and mercy.

review.arabic: رَبِّ اغْفِرْ لِي وَلِوَالِدَيَّ وَلِمَنْ دَخَلَ بَيْتِيَ مُؤْمِنًا وَلِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتِ وَلَا تَزِدِ الظَّالِمِينَ إِلَّا تَبَارًا
review.meaning: Nūḥ prayed for forgiveness for himself, his parents and the believers; the concluding plea against wrongdoers belongs to its historical context.

synthesis.text: Prophet Nūḥ’s account begins with a message: worship Allah alone and turn away from wrongdoing. It continues through long perseverance, different forms of sincere invitation, supplication for forgiveness, and reminders of Allah’s creation. It tells of rejection and mockery; of the command to build the Ark; of Allah’s decree during the Flood; of a father’s grief; and of the Ark resting on al-Jūdī. These events are far greater than any classroom project. The children’s activities help them practise limited ethical lessons while the revealed account retains its full religious meaning.

What should Imaan and Akhlaq carry forward? They can recognize a true message and ask careful questions. They can try again when learning is hard, and adapt their method without becoming dishonest. They can respect people whose possessions or abilities differ from their own. They can remember Allah in gratitude, ask Him for forgiveness, and take responsibility for their actions. They can respond to mockery without cruelty, listen to wise safety guidance, and treat sorrow with compassion.
Ten carry-forward commitments
When I hear something important, I will check that it is true.
When I face a difficulty, I will try one constructive next step.
When someone struggles to understand, I will explain without humiliation.
When I make a mistake, I will seek forgiveness and make amends.
When I see a blessing, I will thank Allah for it.
When someone lacks what I have, I will never treat that person as less worthy.
When a task matters, I will prepare and work carefully.
When someone mocks me, I will avoid revenge and seek help if needed.
When safety matters, I will follow verified guidance from trusted adults.
When a hard chapter passes, I will practise gratitude and begin the next task well.

Mastery standard: A learner can accurately identify the core Qur’anic events, distinguish revelation from imagined classroom storytelling, choose a compassionate action in everyday life, and revisit confusing answers without shame.
